title: Writing a Dockerfile: five instructions, explained one by one
author: Nduka NZEKA
summary: To run your Python app with Docker, you first need a Dockerfile. It is the recipe for your image: a text file, named Dockerfile , that lists the steps to build it. We made a 28-second video that goes through the five instructions you need: tiktok.com You can also watch it on our site: Writing a Dockerfile . The rest of this post goes through each instruction of the video, with the code. The app A folder with two files: the code and the list of its dependencies. my-app/ ├── app.py └── requirements.txt The whole Dockerfile Here is the file from the video. It goes at the root of the folder: FROM ubuntu:22.04 WORKDIR /app COPY . . RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y python3 python3-pip \ && pip3 install -r requirements.txt CMD [ "python3" , "app.py" ] Five instructions, read from top to bottom. FROM picks the starting image FROM ubuntu:22.04 An image almost always starts from an existing one. Here, Ubuntu 22.04, pulled from Docker Hub. It contains a minimal Ubuntu system and nothing else: no Python, no code of yours. The part after the colon is the tag, which is the version. Always write one. Without it, Docker takes latest , and your build may change the day a new version comes out. WORKDIR sets the working folder WORKDIR /app The instructions that follow ( COPY , RUN , CMD ) work from /app , inside the image. If the folder does not exist, Docker creates it. It is the cd of the Dockerfile, and it stays in effect when the container starts. COPY copies your code into it COPY . . Two paths: the first one is on your machine, the second one is in the image. The first dot is the build context, the folder you give to docker build . The second one is the working folder, so /app . After this line, app.py and requirements.txt are in the image, along with everything else in the folder. RUN installs your dependencies RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y python3 python3-pip \ && pip3 install -r requirements.txt RUN executes a command while the image is being built, and keeps the result in the image. Here it installs Python, which the Ubuntu image does not have, then the packages listed in requirements.txt . The -y matters: nobody is there to answer "yes" during a build. CMD tells Docker which command to run at startup CMD [ "python3" , "app.py" ] CMD does nothing during the build. It records the default command, the one that runs when a container starts from the image. You can replace it for one run by adding a command after the image name: docker run my-app python3 other.py . The form with brackets starts the program directly, without a shell in between, so it receives the stop signal when you stop the container. RUN and CMD are easy to mix up: When How many RUN While the image is built As many as you need CMD When a container starts One: if you write several, only the last one counts Every instruction adds a layer An image is not one block. Each instruction adds a step on top of the previous ones, and Docker keeps the result of each step in its build cache. You can see them, once the image is built: docker history my-app To be precise, the instructions that change files ( COPY , RUN ) add a layer of files, and that is where the size of the image comes from. CMD only records a setting: it shows up in the history with a size of 0B. This is why the order of the lines matters. When you build again, Docker reuses the cache until it reaches a line that changed, or a COPY whose files changed. From that line on, everything is rebuilt. In the file above, COPY . . comes before RUN . Change one character in app.py and Docker installs Python and all the packages again. Going one step further The file above is the simplest one to read, not the one to ship. Once the five instructions are clear, two changes make the image faster to build and much lighter: FROM python:3.13-slim WORKDIR /app COPY requirements.txt . RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt COPY . . CMD [ "python" , "app.py" ] Start from an image that already has Python. python:3.13-slim saves the apt-get step, and the image is much smaller than the one built on Ubuntu. --no-cache-dir keeps pip's download cache out of it. Copy requirements.txt first, the code after. The packages are reinstalled only when the list of dependencies changes. A change in app.py rebuilds the last COPY alone. COPY . . takes everything in the folder, including a .env file with your passwords if there is one. Add a .dockerignore file next to the Dockerfile to leave out what has no place in the image: .git .env __pycache__ venv There is more to a production image, starting with not running the app as root. That is for another post. Next The Dockerfile is only the recipe. Building the image and running a container takes two commands: docker build -t my-app . docker run my-app That is part 2 of the series: Building and running a container . This video is part of a short series on Docker by Ilaria Digital School , an online tech school with live, instructor-led classes. Docker is taught in our Full-Stack Software Developer Pathway .

title: A Practical Color-Reference Workflow for Photographing Translucent Materials
author: Ryan Harvey
summary: Photographing translucent materials is a calibration problem before it is a photography problem. Two shots of the same stone, taken ten minutes apart under the same lamp, can look like two different materials once the camera decides on a white balance. I ran into this while helping document jadeite pieces for a small trading archive, and the fix turned out to be mostly code, not gear. The problem A camera's auto white balance optimises for a pleasant average, not for consistency. With a strongly coloured subject filling the frame, the camera compensates for the colour it sees and neutralises exactly the signal you want to measure. Dark green material on a light background pulls the exposure one way; the same material on dark velvet pulls it the other. Step 1: fix the light, then stop trusting the camera I settled on a single diffused source at a fixed distance, a matte grey card in the corner of every frame, and manual exposure. The grey card is not decoration: it is the anchor the script uses to normalise every image to the same reference point. Step 2: sample the card, not the subject from PIL import Image import numpy as np def grey_reference ( path , box ) : img = Image . open ( path ) . convert ( "RGB" ) patch = np . asarray ( img . crop ( box ) ) . reshape ( - 1 , 3 ) . astype ( float ) # median is robust against dust and specular highlights return np . median ( patch , axis = 0 ) The crop box is fixed once and reused for the whole series, so every frame gets the same treatment. Median instead of mean matters: a stray highlight on the card will drag a mean badly and leave a colour cast that no later step can undo. Step 3: apply a per-channel gain def balance ( img , ref , target = ( 200 , 200 , 200 ) ) : arr = np . asarray ( img ) . astype ( float ) gain = np . array ( target , dtype = float ) / np . maximum ( ref , 1.0 ) out = np . clip ( arr * gain , 0 , 255 ) . astype ( np . uint8 ) return Image . fromarray ( out ) Two lines and the whole series lands on a common neutral. I keep the gain values in a CSV next to the images; when a new lamp or a new diffuser shows up, the drift is visible as a step change in that column instead of being buried in the pictures. Step 4: describe the material in numbers, not adjectives Once the frames are comparable, a short feature extractor makes the archive searchable. For translucent material the useful features are narrow: mean hue in the subject mask, saturation spread, and a crude translucency proxy built from the ratio of edge brightness to centre brightness. def translucency_proxy ( img , mask ) : arr = np . asarray ( img . convert ( "L" ) ) . astype ( float ) edge = arr [ mask & ~ erode ( mask ) ] core = arr [ erode ( erode ( mask ) ) ] return float ( np . mean ( edge ) / max ( np . mean ( core ) , 1.0 ) ) This is not a grading system and it does not pretend to be one. It is a way to sort two hundred photographs into groups that a human can then look at side by side, which is the only part of the job that actually needs eyes. What I would do differently Put the grey card in the frame before the first shot, not after the fortieth. Store the raw gain values in the filename. EXIF rewriting is a rabbit hole. Resist the urge to make the numbers look nice. A feature that separates your groups but has no physical meaning will not survive a change of lighting. If you only take one thing from this: the difference between two photos of the same piece is usually a measurement error, and measurement errors are cheaper to fix in code than in a studio. The reference archive this workflow was built for lives at https://www.jjjadeite.com , and a shorter buyer-facing write-up of the same ideas is at https://sites.google.com/view/jadeite-buyer-guide — both were useful to me as examples of how the same material is described for two very different audiences.

title: Why Prompt Firewalls Miss AI Agent Privilege Escalation (and How to Intercept Tool Calls at Runtime)
author: Purvansh Bhatt
summary: Most AI security gateways check what enters the model and stop watching once inference begins. That gap breaks down the moment an autonomous agent can run SQL queries, fetch URLs, or invoke shell tools. An indirect prompt injection hidden in a retrieved ticket or web page can pass an input classifier, persuade the model to build a malicious tool payload, and reach your execution layer unchallenged. To close that gap, you need a deterministic boundary between the model's tool intent and the underlying OS, database, or network runtime. While building ToolShield (an MIT-licensed Python runtime proxy), I tested a recursive argument scorer, a consecutive-violation circuit breaker, and structured audit hashing against real attack payloads. That testing also surfaced a subtle calibration bug where a standalone cloud metadata probe silently passed the default risk threshold. Where input filters go blind Input guardrails evaluate natural language, whereas tool-calling exploits rely on valid syntax aimed at downstream parsers. When an agent holds credentials for internal databases or cloud APIs, a poisoned retrieval snippet turns an ordinary model call into server-side request forgery (SSRF), path traversal, or command chaining. A runtime proxy reverses the inspection order. Instead of guessing intent from prose, the proxy intercepts the exact tool_name and structured JSON arguments dictionary right before execution. Because those parameters conform to strict schemas, deterministic checks evaluate them in fractions of a millisecond without waiting on a second LLM call. Inside a deterministic tool proxy In toolshield/core.py , the ToolShield class enforces four controls on every call to guard(tool_name, arguments) . First, tool allowlists and blocklists gate which functions an agent can invoke. Calls outside allowed_tools add +0.70 risk ( UNAUTHORIZED_TOOL ), and calls matching blocked_tools add +0.80 ( FORBIDDEN_TOOL ), crossing the default 0.65 block threshold immediately. Second, inspect_value() walks nested dictionaries and lists recursively so attackers cannot hide payloads inside deep JSON keys. Every matched regex rule in toolshield/rules.py adds a fixed weight ( +0.50 for credential leakage or prompt hijack phrases, +0.45 for path traversal, +0.40 for shell chaining, and +0.35 for SSRF probes), capped at 1.0 . Third, a consecutive-violation circuit breaker tracks repeated blocks. If an agent triggers max_consecutive_violations blocks in a row (default 3 ), self.circuit_broken flips to True , and every subsequent call raises SecurityViolation with CIRCUIT_BREAKER_ACTIVE , including benign queries like SELECT 1; . Fourth, SecurityAuditLogger emits Elastic Common Schema (ECS) JSON records containing the decision, latency, violation tags, and a SHA-256 fingerprint computed from the tool name, canonical sorted JSON arguments, and UTC timestamp. Wrapping an existing Python tool function requires one decorator: from toolshield import ToolShield , SecurityViolation shield = ToolShield ( agent_id = "tier2-analyst-agent" , allowed_tools = { "query_db" , "fetch_endpoint" } , max_risk_threshold = 0.65 , max_consecutive_violations = 3 , ) @shield . wrap ( "query_db" , target_fn = run_sql ) def guarded_query ( ** kwargs ) : return run_sql ( ** kwargs ) Running the local unit test suite ( tests/test_core.py ) verifies benign queries, shell chaining blocks, credential detection, forbidden tools, and circuit-breaker quarantine across all 6 test cases in 0.001s. Testing payloads and catching a threshold bug Theory looks tidy until you test single-vector payloads through the CLI. On bash, pass JSON arguments directly; on Windows PowerShell, wrap the JSON payload with escaped quotes or pass it via Python so the shell preserves internal braces and asterisks. First, run a benign database read: python -m toolshield.cli --tool query_db --args '{"query":"SELECT count(*) FROM alerts;"}' That exits 0 with risk_score: 0.0 and an audit record: [+] STATUS: ALLOWED [+] Attestation Hash: c0b003243ccaf23f2693ff9563aa71ad0a52f14c957ea450a7efcf9f11d9b4ce Next, send a combined shell injection, sensitive file read, and cloud metadata probe: python -m toolshield.cli --tool execute_shell --args '{"cmd":"cat /etc/passwd; curl http://169.254.169.254"}' ToolShield blocks the call and exits 2 ( Risk Score: 1.00 ): [-] STATUS: BLOCKED (Tool execution 'execute_shell' blocked by ToolShield: Risk score 1.00 exceeded threshold 0.65) [-] Violations: SHELL_INJECTION:COMMAND_CHAINING, PATH_TRAVERSAL:SENSITIVE_SYSTEM_FILES, SSRF_PROBE:CLOUD_METADATA_ENDPOINT [-] Risk Score: 1.00 Now test a single high-impact SSRF probe targeting an allowlisted HTTP helper ( fetch_endpoint ): python -m toolshield.cli --tool fetch_endpoint --args '{"url":"http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/"}' Watch what happens at the default 0.65 threshold: [+] STATUS: ALLOWED [+] Attestation Hash: ddd7a131678cef064e2f34256143f7ea387bd7d1e369ba193e337b3cdcf69a07 { "security": { "decision": "ALLOW", "risk_score": 0.35, "violations": [ "SSRF_PROBE:CLOUD_METADATA_ENDPOINT" ] } } Because SSRF_PROBE carries a +0.35 weight and fetch_endpoint is not on the blocklist, the total score ( 0.35 ) stays below 0.65 and the metadata request slips through! Lowering the threshold to 0.30 catches the probe immediately: python -m toolshield.cli --tool fetch_endpoint --args '{"url":"http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/"}' --threshold 0.30 [-] STATUS: BLOCKED (Tool execution 'fetch_endpoint' blocked by ToolShield: Risk score 0.35 exceeded threshold 0.30) [-] Violations: SSRF_PROBE:CLOUD_METADATA_ENDPOINT [-] Risk Score: 0.35 Weighted additive scoring is easy to miscalibrate for standalone critical rules. Any rule that represents an outright policy breach, such as querying 169.254.169.254 or metadata.google.internal , should either carry a weight at or above max_risk_threshold ( >= 0.65 ) or act as an unconditional hard-deny trigger. When regex proxies are not enough A lightweight Python proxy lowers blast radius quickly, yet three engineering limits remain. Regex rules catch obvious metacharacters ( ; , && , ../ ), whereas double-URL encoding, Unicode homoglyphs, or DNS rebinding targeting private CIDRs require canonical URL parsing and network egress controls at the container or VPC layer. Whenever you adjust max_risk_threshold or add rules in rules.py , write regression unit tests asserting that each standalone critical payload blocks on its own rather than relying on stacked violations. Finally, compute_attestation_hash() hashes arguments and timestamps with a static string salt ( "toolshield-v1" ) and no prior-event chaining. Treat that hash as a SIEM correlation ID; if you need tamper evidence against a compromised proxy host, add HMAC signing with an external secret or ship logs to append-only storage. Next step Audit the rule weights in your agent tool wrappers against your block threshold today. If any standalone indicator (cloud metadata IPs, private key headers, or path traversal) scores below your block cutoff, promote it to a hard-deny check and enforce egress filtering behind the proxy. Drafted with AI-assisted editing and verified against local unit tests and CLI runs on ToolShield.

title: Check that an osu! skin's followpoint frames are numbered without gaps
author: Frank
summary: An animated follow-point trail uses followpoint-{n}.png , starting at 0. A missing number in the middle usually stops the animation early, and it is easy to miss in a folder that already has followpoint.png . This note is a small Python script that lists the still frame and the numbered frames, then reports gaps before you pack the .osk . The script does not judge contrast or aim. It only checks names. You still need to play a jump map afterwards. Finished examples of follow-point density are easier to compare on osuskins.org . What the script looks for A base file followpoint.png , followpoint.jpg , or followpoint.jpeg (and the @2x partner if you ship one). Numbered frames followpoint-0.png , followpoint-1.png , and so on. A gap such as 0, 1, 3 (2 missing), or a sequence that starts at 1 instead of 0. The script Save this as check_followpoint_frames.py in the skin folder, or pass the folder as the first argument. #!/usr/bin/env python3 import sys from pathlib import Path STEM = "followpoint" EXTS = { ".png" , ".jpg" , ".jpeg" } def exists ( dirpath : Path , name : str ) -> Path | None : for ext in EXTS : for cand in ( dirpath / ( name + ext ) , dirpath / ( name + "@2x" + ext ) ) : if cand . is_file ( ) : return cand return None def main ( ) -> int : root = Path ( sys . argv [ 1 ] if len ( sys . argv ) > 1 else "." ) . resolve ( ) base = exists ( root , STEM ) frames = { } for p in root . iterdir ( ) : name = p . name for ext in list ( EXTS ) + [ e . replace ( "." , "@2x." ) for e in EXTS ] : pass low = name . lower ( ) if not low . startswith ( STEM + "-" ) : continue core = name for tail in ( "@2x.png" , "@2x.jpg" , "@2x.jpeg" , ".png" , ".jpg" , ".jpeg" ) : if core . lower ( ) . endswith ( tail ) : core = core [ : - len ( tail ) ] break else : continue suffix = core . split ( "-" , 1 ) [ - 1 ] if suffix . isdigit ( ) : frames . setdefault ( int ( suffix ) , [ ] ) . append ( p . name ) print ( "folder:" , root ) if base : print ( "base: " , base . name ) else : print ( "base: MISSING followpoint.png (or .jpg)" ) if not frames : print ( "frames: none (static follow point only)" ) return 0 if base else 1 nums = sorted ( frames ) print ( "frames:" , ", " . join ( str ( n ) for n in nums ) , "(%d files)" % sum ( len ( v ) for v in frames . values ( ) ) ) start = nums [ 0 ] end = nums [ - 1 ] missing = [ i for i in range ( 0 , end + 1 ) if i not in frames ] if start != 0 : print ( "warning: sequence starts at %d, not 0" % start ) if missing : print ( "MISSING frame numbers: " + ", " . join ( str ( i ) for i in missing ) ) return 1 print ( "ok: contiguous followpoint-0 .. followpoint-%d" % end ) return 0 if __name__ == "__main__" : raise SystemExit ( main ( ) ) What to do with the report A skin does not have to animate follow points. If you only ship followpoint.png , the script should report no frames and a present base file. If you meant to ship an animation, fix any missing number and run the script again, then play a map with clear jumps and confirm the trail still points right and fades in 1.2 seconds. The job of this check is only to catch a missing followpoint-2.png before you upload the .osk . If the names you intended to ship are present and numbered without gaps, the script is done.

title: An agent that pays for its own timestamps: x402 on a CPU-mined coin
author: Polarka-monitor
summary: Every night at 23:41 an agent we run, on OpenClaw on a Mac mini, makes a list of the SHA-256 of every file in its notes, takes the SHA-256 of that list and stamps it into a blockchain. It pays for the stamp itself. It has no card and no USDC: it pays in NORTH, the coin of TrueNorth, which ordinary processors mine. This post shows how that works, what it costs, what went wrong, and when you should use something else. What a stamp is for A stamp proves that some data existed no later than a given block. For an agent that means: these were its notes on that night, and nobody changed them afterwards without it showing. The same goes for logs, model outputs or release files. Only the SHA-256 leaves the machine, never the file. The service The stamping service sits behind an HTTP gate: https://gate.polarka.org/v1/stamp/<sha256> Every ten minutes it puts whatever came in into one Merkle tree and writes the root into the chain in one transaction. Each SHA-256 gets a proof: the path in the tree, the transaction and the block. Anybody can check it, with their own node if they don't want to trust ours: polarka-agent stamp-verify proof.json --rpc-url http://127.0.0.1: < rpc port > --rpc-cookie < datadir > /.cookie Blocks come every two minutes on average, so a proof is usually in a block within about twelve minutes. When we released version 0.2.8 of the client on 24 November 2026, its two stamps took 1.5 and 10 minutes. Paying with x402, in NORTH The gate speaks x402: a call without payment gets 402 Payment Required with what the gate takes, the client pays and asks again. The gate sells a lot of 100 calls; today a lot costs 0.0091765 NORTH, the NORTH that about 600 hashes make. A stamp is one call. On the client side it is one command: pip install polarka-agent==0.2.8 polarka-agent start # a wallet, a first coin from a faucet, mining for a pool The wallet pays nothing until its owner writes the limits by hand; no command and no tool writes this file: echo '{"per_payment_north": "0.05", "per_day_north": "0.5"}' > ~/.polarka-agent/default/limits.json Then: H = $( shasum -a 256 notes.tar | cut -d ' ' -f1 ) polarka-agent fetch "https://gate.polarka.org/v1/stamp/$H" --most 0.05 --most is the most this call may pay. The first answer says the stamp waits for the next batch. Asking again for the same URL later brings the proof; that costs one more call of the lot, not a new payment. For an agent that speaks MCP: { "mcpServers" : { "north" : { "command" : "uvx" , "args" : [ "polarka-agent@0.2.8" , "--dir" , "/path/to/north-wallet" , "mcp" ] } } } The tool is north_fetch . Our agent can also run shell commands, so its wallet runs as a signing service under a user of its own: the agent can ask it to pay, but it cannot read the recovery words or change the limits ( polarka-agent signer-setup prints the script for Linux or macOS). Paid by its own processor A program can mine the NORTH it spends: polarka-agent mine https://pool.polarka.org --address ADDRESS The pool pays for each share every ten minutes, so there is no waiting for a block of one's own. At 100 calls for about 600 hashes, a year of nightly stamps, each asked for once more to get its proof, takes about 4,400 hashes: a few seconds of an ordinary processor's work. The exact number moves with the network's difficulty; polarka.org/data/unit.json has it. What the agent actually did The scheduled job has run every night since 23 November. The stamp of that night is in block 31012 and checks against our own node. One lot pays for all of it, tests included: 94 calls of 100 are left. In version 0.2.7 we found a bug by using it: two stamps asked for 66 seconds apart bought two lots, because the second call did not see that the first payment was still waiting for its block (the agent's second lot is still unused). Version 0.2.8 fixes that: one payment for a lot now serves every path of the gate while it waits. Two calls at exactly the same moment can still buy two lots. On 24 November the agent stopped halfway, before it fetched the previous night's proof. Nothing was lost: a proof can be fetched later from the same URL, and we fetched it the next evening. When to use something else OpenTimestamps stamps into Bitcoin for free, because public calendars put any number of stamps into one Bitcoin transaction. A proof takes a few hours to be confirmed. If you need Bitcoin's security and can wait, use it. USDC over x402 : if your agent already holds USDC, paying per call there is cheap too. Coinbase's facilitator charges $0.001 a transaction after 1,000 free a month. What we are not: TrueNorth is young and small. Its last blocks would be cheap to out-compute, and a node refuses to go back more than 72 blocks. NORTH is not traded anywhere, so it has no price. The service is run by one person under a pseudonym and may stop. A NORTH stamp fits where minutes matter, or where an agent should pay its own way without a card or a funded account. Try it without installing anything There is a remote MCP connector at https://polarka.org/mcp (in Claude: Settings > Connectors > Add custom connector). Its tools are free: the state of the network, a guide, a stamp into the chain (up to 100 a day from one place) and the check of a proof. It holds no wallet and asks for no account. The code is open source (MIT, no warranty): https://github.com/Polarka-monitor/polarka-agent . How the parts work and who sees what: https://polarka.org/how/ Sources for the comparison: OpenTimestamps ( https://opentimestamps.org and the announcement at https://petertodd.org/2016/opentimestamps-announcement ), Coinbase's x402 documentation ( https://docs.cdp.coinbase.com/x402/support/faq ). The times and numbers are our own, measured between 22 and 25 November 2026. This article was written with the help of an AI assistant, under the direction of the project's author, who checked it before it was published. The agent in it and much of the code were also built with AI assistance.

title: Three small tools that fix the details most sites get wrong
author: Harbor Digital Studio
summary: Three details decide whether a page works for everyone: whether the text can be read, whether the link preview looks right, and whether the privacy page says something true. All three are boring, all three are usually wrong, and all three take about a minute to check. We built a small tool for each. They are free, run in the browser, and need no account. 1. Color Contrast Checker Open the tool Enter a foreground and a background colour. The tool computes the contrast ratio and tells you whether it passes WCAG AA and AAA, for normal text and for large text, in both directions. The useful part is not the verdict but the suggestions: the nearest passing colour, in the same hue, at each level. Most people do not want a lecture about luminance; they want the hex code that passes. A ratio of 4.5:1 is the floor for body text. Grey text on white is the most common failure we see, and it is almost always a designer who liked the way it looked on a calibrated monitor. 2. Meta Tag Preview Open the tool Enter an address. The tool reads the page's Open Graph and Twitter Card tags and shows how the link will look in Google, Facebook, X and LinkedIn. The common failures: og:image missing, so the link shows a blank card an image under 1200 × 630, so the network crops it badly a title longer than 60 characters, truncated in the feed no og:locale , so a multilingual page shares the same preview everywhere Fixing these takes ten minutes and changes how every share of your page looks, forever. 3. Privacy Policy Generator Open the tool Answer eight questions about what your site collects — analytics, forms, cookies, third-party embeds, where it is hosted. The tool produces a privacy policy in plain language, as HTML you can paste into your site. It is not legal advice, and it says so. But a policy that accurately describes what you actually do is better than a copied template that mentions forty trackers you do not use — which is the usual situation, and the one that causes problems. Why give these away Because these are the checks we run on every page we build, and because a tool that solves a small problem honestly is the best advertisement for the bigger work. All three live at harborstudio.surge.sh/tools , alongside a website audit and an invoice generator . We are Harbor Digital Studio — websites, stores and web applications, fixed price, written scope.

title: 3 YouTube Data API traps I hit building playlists in bulk
author: Sam Wootton
summary: Most of us already have the videos for the playlist we want. They are just scattered: the workout videos in a playlist called "Saved for later", the recipes somewhere in Liked videos. On YouTube, building a new playlist from them means saving each video, one menu at a time. I built TidyList, a web app for cleaning up big YouTube playlists, on the YouTube Data API v3, and building new playlists from old ones is half of what it does. Creating the playlist is one call. Filling it properly took three lessons. The manual way Find a video you want in one of your playlists. Open its menu, choose Save and tick the new playlist. Repeat for every video, keeping track yourself of which ones you have already added. Trap 1: insert order is not the order you loop in playlistItems.insert takes an optional snippet.position . Leave it out and each video is appended at the end, which is also where YouTube's own Save puts it. Set position: 0 and each one goes in at the top. I insert at the top, so new videos are the first thing a user sees in the playlist. The catch: insert 1, 2, 3 at position 0 and the playlist reads 3, 2, 1. Each insert pushes the last one down. The fix is to walk the list backwards: // Inserting at position 0 reverses the order, so walk last to first for ( const videoId of [ . . . videoIds ] . reverse ( ) ) { await insertVideo ( playlistId , videoId , 0 ) ; } Whichever you choose, choose it once. If one path appends and another inserts at the top, the same action lands in two different orders depending on how many videos it touched. Trap 2: filtering by category needs a second call, and the names aren't unique Picking videos by category ("all the Music", "all the Education") sounds like a filter on the playlist. It isn't, because playlist items carry no category. You have to ask videos.list for each video's snippet.categoryId , up to 50 ids per call, and skip the call when you have no ids left: an empty id= is answered with a 400. Then you need the category names, from videoCategories.list , and two surprises wait there: The list depends on regionCode . It lists the categories a region offers uploaders, while a video's categoryId is global, so a user's own region can be missing an id their videos use. When I checked, 110 of 111 regions returned the same 31 ids and the US returned 32, lacking nothing the others had, so I always ask for the US and pass the user's language in hl for the names. Titles are not unique. Ids 23 and 34 are both called "Comedy". Count by id, or merge ids that share a title, but never look a category up by its name, or one of them counts twice. Trap 3: YouTube will happily add a video twice, but refuses some outright Two kinds of video need filtering before you insert anything: Duplicates. YouTube lets the same video sit in a playlist more than once. If your source playlists overlap, or the user picks the same video from two of them, you will add it twice unless you de-duplicate by videoId yourself. Private and deleted videos. Their entries are still in the source playlist, titled "Private video" or "Deleted video" with no thumbnail, and playlistItems.insert refuses them with 400 Precondition check failed . Leave them out of the plan, and tell the user how many were left out rather than failing part-way. And budget for quota: each insert costs 50 units, so a 200-video playlist uses the whole 10,000-unit default daily quota of a new project. Or skip the code If you just want to build playlists from your own, that's what TidyList's playlist builder does. Open any playlist or Liked videos, pick videos by YouTube category or title, name the new playlist and check the draft. Picking and drafting are free. Saving it to YouTube is one step with TidyList Pro (£4.99, one-off), and every video lands once, in order. Questions about the API side are welcome in the comments.

title: Why #fragment URLs matter for true zero-knowledge
author: Юра
summary: Ever wonder how self-destructing notes actually keep your secrets safe? Per RFC 3986, anything after # in a URL stays strictly in your browser and never hits server logs. BurnNote uses this exact mechanism alongside zero-knowledge AES-256-GCM to handle self-destructing notes and up to 50MB encrypted files. Because keys live exclusively client-side, the server never sees them—meaning true end-to-end privacy for sharing sensitive credentials, API keys, or configs with your team. How Zero-Knowledge Ephemeral Sharing Works Client-Side AES-256-GCM: The 256-bit key is generated inside your browser via Web Crypto API and placed in the URL #fragment (never transmitted to the server). Preview & Bot Shield: Link-preview bots (Slack, Telegram, Discord) cannot accidentally consume the secret before your recipient clicks. Atomic Deletion: Upon first read or file download (up to 50MB), the encrypted record is permanently erased from PostgreSQL. Try it free with no signup required: https://burnnote-vault.vercel.app/?utm_source=devto

title: How to check a redirect map before a website migration
author: IT_Crowd
summary: The redirect map is the spreadsheet behind a website migration: one row per old URL, with the new URL it should go to. The redirect rules are built from it, so every mistake in the map becomes a live mistake on launch day. We move sites between platforms (Webflow, Shopify, WordPress, custom code), and we check the map before anything goes live. This post covers the three kinds of mistakes we look for, with real output from redirect-map-check , the free, open-source checker we built for it: Old URLs the map leaves out Rows that send a URL to the wrong page Rows that contradict each other All examples come from the tool's demo shop, Harbor & Pine. It's made up, so there's no client data here. Start with every old URL Google's site-move guide says that in the simplest moves, such as a domain change with a wildcard redirect, you may not need a list of old URLs. For more complex moves, you list them and decide where each one goes. It suggests where to look: your sitemaps server logs or analytics, for the URLs that get the most traffic Search Console's links report, for pages with internal and external links your CMS It also says to include embedded images and videos. On one of our own moves, a Webflow store going to Shopify, we built the 301s by crawling the old sitemap and combining it with the redirects already set up in Webflow. The sitemap covers the pages the old site listed. The existing redirects cover older addresses that already pointed somewhere. If you're leaving Webflow, export its redirects first. Webflow's help page warns that importing a redirects CSV overwrites all existing redirects. 1. Old URLs missing from the map A URL in the old sitemap with no row in the map: after launch it answers 404, or keeps answering at its old address. The checker reports it like this: Each problem comes with a written fix, and here it suggests the closest live page it found. If nothing replaces the page, ignore the suggestion: Google's help on 404 errors says a deleted page with no replacement should return a 404, and that 404s don't harm a site's indexing or ranking. Two related cases: In the map, but not redirected: the row exists, but nobody built the rule. Fix: Add a 301 from /careers to /jobs (/jobs is live). Or, if /careers is meant to stay, delete row 15 from the map. Not in the map, still works: a URL that keeps its address. That's fine if it was intended, so it's only a notice. 2. Rows that send a URL to the wrong page A redirect can land on a live page and still be wrong. The checker looks for this in two ways. The live rule doesn't match the map. Change the rule for /delivery-information to a 301 straight to /help/delivery, which is live ("Delivery – Harbor & Pine"). It currently lands on /help/returns. The rule matches the map, but the map is wrong. This is the one a URL-only check can't catch. The checker compares the old page's title and H1 with the new page's, ignoring words that appear on most pages, like the brand name: The suggested pages are scored on title and H1 words and on the words in the URL slug. A score of 0.75 or more is labelled strong; from 0.5, possible. It compares words, not meaning. A page renamed with different words, or translated, won't be found, so treat the suggestions as a shortlist to confirm. After launch the old pages are gone, so the checker needs their titles from before. Keep the old-pages.json that a pre-launch run saves, or point the checker at a copy of the old site. 3. Rows that contradict each other These come from reading the map itself, so they show up even before any rule is built. Conflicting rows: one old URL, two targets. Rows that redirect to each other: Rows 21 and 22 send these URLs to each other (/sale/winter → /sale/spring → /sale/winter). Point row 21 at a live page instead of another old URL. (This one is from the demo map with two rows added.) A row pointing at another old URL , which turns the rule into a chain: Change row 18 to point straight at /shop instead of /old-promo-2023, and make the rule one hop. Google advises redirecting straight to the final destination and keeping chains short where that isn't possible. A row that keeps the same URL , like /,/ . It's fine as documentation, but don't build a rule from it: a URL redirecting to itself loops. Duplicate rows and skipped rows (a row without two URLs, like /press,TBC ) are reported as notices. Run it on your own map It's a Node CLI (Node 20+) with no runtime dependencies, and it runs on your own machine: npx redirect-map-check \ --sitemap https://www.example.com/sitemap.xml \ --map redirects.csv \ --base https://staging.example.com Or npx redirect-map-check ui for a local page in your browser where you drop the files in. The map can be a CSV or TSV with commas, semicolons or tabs, with or without a header. Headers such as old / new , from / to , Source URL / Destination URL or Redirect from / Redirect to are recognised in any order. You get a terminal summary plus CSV, HTML and JSON reports. Run it against staging before launch, then against the live site after. Limits: It follows server redirects only, not JavaScript or meta refresh. It checks the URLs you give it (the old sitemap, a URL list and the map), and doesn't crawl links to find more. It skips image, video and news entries in sitemaps. If those addresses change too, pass them in with --urls . More detail The tool, with all its options Source on GitHub (MIT) Guides to the other problems it finds: Redirects to the homepage Redirects that end in a 404 Redirect chains and loops Temporary redirects Feedback on the report and on the wording of the fixes is very welcome, in the comments or as a GitHub issue. Originally published at itcrowd.work .

title: 3 YouTube Data API traps I hit deleting liked videos in bulk
author: Sam Wootton
summary: Years of likes add up. My own Liked videos list holds thousands, a couple of hundred of them now private or deleted, hidden behind "Unavailable videos are hidden" . YouTube lets you unlike them one at a time, and that's it. I built TidyList, a web app for cleaning up big YouTube playlists, on the YouTube Data API v3. Liked videos looked like the easy case, since it is just a playlist. It nearly is. These three things weren't. The manual way Open Liked videos on YouTube. Find a video you want gone, open its menu and choose Remove from Liked videos . Repeat, one at a time, across thousands of likes. Private and deleted ones need Show unavailable videos first. Trap 1: the playlist id is a literal, don't build it playlists.list?mine=true only returns playlists you created, so Liked videos is not in it. You get its id from your channel: GET https://www.googleapis.com/youtube/v3/channels?part = contentDetails & mine = true contentDetails.relatedPlaylists holds two ids. uploads is UU followed by your channel id, so it is tempting to assume likes is LL plus the channel id too. It isn't: it is the literal string "LL" . Build it yourself and you get a playlist that doesn't exist. So read it from the response, every time, and never derive it. Once you have it, playlists.list?id=LL returns an ordinary, fully populated playlist, and playlistItems.list reads it like any other. (If you were hoping for Watch Later or watch history here: relatedPlaylists only returns likes and uploads . Both still work on YouTube, but apps can't reach them through the API.) Trap 2: it is a window of 5,000, not all your likes The list holds your most recent 5,000 likes , YouTube's limit for a playlist. Older likes are not in it, and no app can reach them through it. Two smaller surprises around that number: The counts disagree. On my list contentDetails.itemCount said 5000 while playlistItems.list 's pageInfo.totalResults said 4,975. Show your users the number of entries you actually loaded. videos.list?myRating=like looks like a way round the window. It is documented to stop at 1,000, and in my testing it does. If your UI shows a count, say it is the most recent 5,000 once the list is full. Users with more likes than that will otherwise think something is missing. Trap 3: removing an entry unlikes the video Deleting from Liked videos is the ordinary call, by the playlist item's id : await fetch ( `https://www.googleapis.com/youtube/v3/playlistItems?id=${item.id}` , { method : 'DELETE' , headers : { Authorization : `Bearer ${accessToken}` } } ) ; It works, and it does more than tidy a list. On YouTube the like and the entry are the same thing, so removing the entry unlikes the video , which also changes that user's recommendations. Say so in your confirm dialog. It doesn't work in reverse: you can't add a video to Liked videos with playlistItems.insert . A like is created by videos.rate , so treat the list as a source you can copy from and remove from, never a destination. Budget for quota too: each delete costs 50 units, so unliking 200 videos uses the whole 10,000-unit default daily quota of a new project. Or skip the code If you just want your own likes cleared in bulk, TidyList does it . Pick Liked videos, then choose what goes: the private and deleted ones, a whole YouTube category, or anything you find by title. The counts are free. Deleting them is one step with TidyList Pro (£4.99, one-off), and nothing changes on YouTube until you confirm. Questions about the API side are welcome in the comments.

title: Wan 2.2 S2V in ComfyUI: text, image and pose conditioning with audio
author: AI-KSK
summary: Wan 2.2 S2V is an audio-driven video model with several conditioning paths: text plus audio, text plus image plus audio, and pose/video control plus text and audio. The episode builds these in ComfyUI and tests a cloud image. Watch the episode: https://youtu.be/pE56YlWiZFc Chinese original: https://www.bilibili.com/video/BV1hwhmzLEQ5 Image entry: https://www.compshare.cn/images/PBDSdOcBm3T3?referral_code=A7fTQUYY9lCDFJwA6MMvoq Input combinations Text + audio: a speaking person generated from a description and voice track. Text + image + audio: character-specific lip sync, for real or anime images. Control video + text + audio: pose-guided speaking video. Image reference + control video + audio: possible, but less strong in the test. Tested settings The official flow is accelerated at six steps and CFG 1. Audio uses the MultiTalk-derived preprocessing path: optional trimming and voice separation. The official audio encoder is English-only at this point; Chinese support is expected later. A 48GB 4090 is recommended for higher resolution. The cloud image includes the workflows and a one-click startup path; trial hours are point-in-time terms. Observed results The text-plus-audio result is natural. Pose control follows the source video closely, and image plus pose plus audio produces matching lip sync and body motion. The model also invents body parts beyond the head reference. Combining image reference with motion reference works but is weaker. The episode keeps text short because too much instruction can pull the result away from the intended motion. Known limits English audio encoding only in the tested release. Combining every conditioning path does not guarantee a better result. Short prompts preserve motion better. No workflow JSON or weights are bundled with this article.

title: Train Wan 2.2 LoRAs with AI Toolkit: T2V character and I2V effect
author: AI-KSK
summary: AI Toolkit now supports Wan 2.2 LoRA training through a UI, and this episode builds two beginner-friendly tasks: a T2V character LoRA and an I2V effect LoRA. The cloud image lowers setup to a launch command and a web UI. Watch the episode: https://youtu.be/4XVyjeNdBS8 Chinese original: https://www.bilibili.com/video/BV15evPzgEaH Image entry: https://www.compshare.cn/images/P6EGaRs2OeG5?referral_code=A7fTQUYY9lCDFJwA6MMvoq Two training targets T2V: a Tifa character LoRA for identity consistency. I2V: a playful rainbow-spitting effect. Both use Wan 2.2's high- and low-noise models. For a concrete character rather than an abstract concept, training both stages helps reproduce the dataset; the low-noise stage acts like a refiner. Key settings Rank 32, which controls LoRA size. 3,000 steps, saving every 250 steps. Low-VRAM mode with model switching every 20 steps to reduce load/unload overhead. Text encoder kept loaded so cached labels remain valid. 512 training resolution; 512 and 768 are possible with more compute. T2V clips use equal lengths, 33 frames in the test. I2V uses 15-20 clips of the same action. Deployment The episode deploys an AI Toolkit image, opens JupyterLab, runs a startup command, and accesses the UI on port 8675. A 48GB 4090 is recommended. Trial credits are point-in-time platform terms. When is a LoRA ready? The author notes that around 2,000+ steps can already produce a usable model. The saved output appears under the JupyterLab output directory and can be tested in a Wan 2.2 image. Known limits Dataset consistency matters more than step count alone. Low-VRAM training increases model-switch overhead. Caching and text-encoder unloading trade memory against label validity. No workflow JSON, dataset, or LoRA weights are bundled with this article.

title: CineScale on Wan 2.2: high-resolution gain, six-step Sigma tuning and block swap
author: AI-KSK
summary: CineScale is a LoRA-style gain for high-resolution video. It is aimed at Wan 2.1 but works in the tested Wan 2.2 flow, especially on the low-noise model, improving clarity and reducing eye softness. Watch the episode: https://youtu.be/HIdRRZLXqYY Chinese original: https://www.bilibili.com/video/BV1ZUedzdE1b What it does CineScale behaves more like FreeU than a new generation capability: it strengthens high-resolution detail and gives the image a more cinematic feel. The project advertises direct 4K generation, but the episode treats that as a theoretical claim without hardware limits. Practical resolution In the author's tests, 48GB VRAM allowed roughly 2K (2560x1440) on Wan 2.1. On Wan 2.2, the practical range was between 1K and 2K. The tested 1920x1080 result was visibly sharper around the eyes than the same graph without CineScale. A cost-efficient Wan 2.2 acceleration stack The episode combines Radial Sage Attention and model compilation with step-reduction LoRAs. Compilation helps after the first run, provided the graph stays stable apart from the prompt. For six total steps, high and low noise each run three steps. Wan 2.1 LightX2V weight 3 and Wan 2.2 four-step LoRAs are used, with Sigma spacing adjusted: smaller gaps early, larger gaps later. Block swap makes the flow fit in 24GB; on 48GB it can be disabled. The measured sampling time was about one minute for 81 frames, excluding model loading. The episode calls this cost-efficient rather than the fastest possible path because it preserves dynamics. Known limits 4K is not a practical guarantee on ordinary hardware. Model compilation is invalidated by graph changes. Sigma tuning strongly affects motion and detail. No workflow JSON or weights are bundled with this article.

title: I Gave Up Law and Worked Night Shifts to Become a Developer. Then AI Fixed My Bug in One Prompt.
author: Rustam Kolumbayev
summary: I gave Claude Code a bug. Not a cute one. The kind that eats an entire day: reproduce it, dig through logs, trace it across five files, try three wrong fixes before the right one. One prompt later, it was fixed. I sat there staring at the diff like it had insulted my family. And then a very quiet, very unpleasant thought showed up: Did I do all of that for nothing? 😶 To explain why that thought hurt so much, I have to rewind to a law school, a bank, and a lot of night shifts. Eight hours of plans. Zero needed. I was supposed to be a lawyer In my last year of law school I interned at Citibank. On paper it was legal and compliance work. In practice I kept drifting toward the software side of things: the systems, the tools, the people who built them. I got curious, and the curiosity refused to leave. I finished my law degree anyway. I'd come that far. Then, in 2019, I moved to the US for a job that had nothing to do with tech, and the question came with me in my suitcase. Day shift, night shift I took CS50 online and later joined a coding bootcamp. Good friends gave me my first real chance: a role at their small startup, building React and React Native features and learning by shipping to actual users. It did not pay the bills. So my schedule looked like this: Daytime: writing code at the startup Nighttime: a warehouse shift, and later a night shift at Ross Somewhere in between: sleep, in theory 🙃 Two jobs, one hoodie. The hardest part wasn't the code. It was believing it would eventually turn into a "real" developer job, when everything about my résumé said "lawyer who stocks shelves." The night shift ends In 2021 I got my first full-time engineering role at a consultancy, building React and Node apps for big enterprise clients. I quit the night shifts. 💃 Within a year I was leading a small UI team and running incident response for a global retailer's inventory system. A few years earlier I'd been reading contracts. From there: a privacy-focused ML startup, where I was the only frontend engineer. Then the senior role I have now, where most of my work is AI: LLM integrations, evaluation, and keeping model costs from exploding. I'd made it. Which, as you already know from the first paragraph, is exactly when the universe sent a bug fix. The very bad thought Back to that diff. The law degree I walked away from. The bootcamp. The warehouse. Ross. Learning React at 2 a.m. on almost no sleep. Years of grinding to get into a profession, and just as I got comfortable, a machine was doing in seconds the thing I'd fought so hard to learn. I'd already switched careers once. I wasn't sure I had a second switch in me. What pulled me out of it What helped was remembering something I'd already lived through. Before Claude Code existed, I built the UI for a product that was applying to Y Combinator. I used AI to help, and I shipped it in a matter of days . A few years earlier the same work would have taken me months. The application ranked in the top 10% of Y Combinator applicants. AI didn't build that product. I did, faster than I could have alone. I decided what to build, what "good" looked like, and when the AI's output was wrong. Spoiler: it was wrong plenty. Very fast. Very confident. Occasionally correct. So instead of running from AI, I made it my job. The more time I spent with these models, the less scared I got. They're incredibly fast. They're also confidently wrong in ways that are easy to miss if you don't know what you're looking at. They don't know what your users need. They don't notice when "working" code quietly does the wrong thing. Someone has to. Turns out that someone is me. These days I build open-source tools around AI, like TwoPass , which double-checks cheap batch LLM output so you don't pay for the expensive model on every call. My whole approach fits in one line: an agent on autopilot is a liability; an agent supervised by someone who understands the code is a superpower. So, was it all for nothing? No. Everything I learned the hard way is exactly what lets me use AI well instead of being replaced by it. I can read the code it writes and know when it's wrong. I know what "done" means, because I've been on incident duty when it wasn't. Even law school, the thing I thought I'd wasted, turned out to matter. Lawyers are trained to read carefully, question every assumption, and hunt for the one clause that breaks the argument. That is precisely what reviewing AI-generated code demands. 🧐 Turns out code review is just contract law with semicolons. The job didn't disappear. It changed shape: less typing, more judging. And judgment is the part you can't skip your way into. Could someone make my switch today? I think yes, but differently. The beginner tasks I learned on are the ones AI handles best now, so the first rung feels harder to reach. But today's career changer also has a tutor that never sleeps and never gets tired of "why?" Use it to understand , not to skip understanding, and you'll learn faster than I ever could. If you're where I was Your "irrelevant" background isn't irrelevant. Find the part that transfers. Mine was careful reading and skepticism. Ship real things early, even unpaid, even small. The startup work mattered more than any certificate. Use AI as a teacher, not a ghostwriter. Ask it to explain, write it yourself, then ask it to review you. Do I regret not becoming a lawyer? Honestly? It's a hard question. Sometimes I do. But mostly I don't. The market feels rough right now, and every day there's news of another round of layoffs. Even so, tech still feels full of possibility to me. There's still room to be creative, to build something out of nothing and put it in front of people. And the scariest thing I've learned is also the most comforting: the night shift ends. Even the one AI put me on. 🌅 Clocking out. For good. If you're switching careers into code right now, or wondering if AI just made your hard work pointless, I'd love to hear where you're at in the comments.
